title: Preface
text:
Welcome
Artificial intelligence can seem like a collection of impressive demonstrations. A chatbot writes a response, a vision model labels an image, or an assistant summarizes a document. The demonstration shows what is possible, but it does not establish whether the system solves a real problem reliably, safely, or at an acceptable cost.
Artificial Intelligence: A Practical Path from AI Concepts to a Working Prototype is an introduction to making those judgments. It explains the ideas behind modern AI, helps you choose an appropriate approach, and guides you through designing, building, evaluating, and communicating a small prototype. You do not need to train a large model to learn how to build a useful AI application.
The principle throughout this guide is:

text: Begin with the user’s task and a measurable definition of success. Choose the simplest suitable approach, test it on representative cases, and make its limitations visible.

title: Preface
text:
A complete open guide
This guide is available as one connected learning pathway. Its chapters provide the concepts and technical steps needed to develop a prototype. CDI practical products may offer additional exercises, project files, datasets, and structured deliverables; the guide itself remains complete and openly available.

title: Preface
text:
Who this guide is for
This guide is intended for people who want to understand and apply AI in research, education, business, or public-interest work. Basic familiarity with Python and using a terminal will help with the hands-on sections. Prior experience with machine learning or large language models is useful but not required.
The examples focus on a small, reviewable use case. You can transfer the workflow to another domain, provided that you reconsider the data, users, errors, and risks in that setting.

title: Preface
Preface
section: What we mean by a prototype
text:
What we mean by a prototype
A prototype is a limited implementation designed to answer a specific question: Can this approach help a defined user complete a defined task under stated conditions? It may be a command-line program, notebook-backed experiment, or small interface. Its purpose is to generate evidence and feedback, not to imply production readiness.
For example, a prototype might help a reviewer find passages in an approved set of documents and draft a cited summary. A useful evaluation would check whether the retrieved passages support the summary, whether the system admits when the documents lack an answer, and how often a reviewer must correct it. A polished interface alone would not answer those questions.

title: Preface
text:
How the guide is organized

Foundations
Chapters 01–03 establish AI thinking and problem framing, explain the roles of data, models, and inference, and clarify how AI relates to machine learning.


Modern AI
Chapters 04–08 introduce neural networks, language models and generative AI, image and multimodal systems, prompting and structured outputs, and workflows that use retrieval and tools. The emphasis is on choosing and testing these capabilities for a specific task.


Building responsibly
Chapters 09–11 develop evaluation and failure analysis, privacy, bias, human oversight, and reproducible AI workflows. These chapters provide the evidence and safeguards needed before presenting a prototype as useful.


AI Hackathon
Chapters 12–14 form a guided build sequence: choose a problem, build and test a focused solution, then present the evidence and improve it. Here, a hackathon means a structured, time-bounded learning project. You can complete it individually or with a team; speed does not excuse weak evaluation or careless data use.


Next steps
Chapter 15 considers how to turn a promising prototype into a more dependable practical application, including what additional testing, documentation, and operational decisions would be required.

title: Preface
text:
The learning workflow
The guide follows a sequence that you can reuse for new AI ideas:

Define the task. Identify the user, the input, the desired output, and the decision or action the output supports.
Set boundaries. Record the data sources, permitted uses, privacy requirements, cost and latency limits, and cases that require a person.
Choose an approach. Compare a simple baseline with an AI method before adding complexity.
Build a small version. Keep components, configuration, prompts, and example inputs easy to inspect.
Evaluate. Use representative examples, explicit criteria, and error review rather than selecting only impressive outputs.
Improve deliberately. Change one part at a time and check whether the change addresses a documented failure.
Communicate the result. Show the working prototype alongside its evidence, limitations, and next steps.

This process is iterative. Evaluation may show that the problem needs a different data source, a narrower task, a simpler method, or more human review.

title: Preface
text:
How to use this guide
Read the conceptual chapters in order if AI is new to you. In each hands-on chapter, first identify the question the example is meant to answer. Then inspect the code, run the corresponding repository script where one is provided, examine the output, and record what worked and what failed. Keep your own test cases separate from examples used to develop prompts or tune the prototype.
Code in the .qmd chapters is illustrative and does not run when the book renders. Complete executable examples belong in scripts/python/, with shell wrappers in scripts/bash/ where appropriate. Run scripts from the repository root, use a repository-specific .venv, and consult requirements.txt for the project’s dependencies. Generated figures and tables, where used, belong under results/figures/ and results/tables/.
Some examples may rely on a hosted AI service. Such examples require the service’s current access terms, credentials, and possible usage charges. Never place an API key or sensitive source material in a chapter, notebook output, screenshot, or committed file. The conceptual and evaluation steps remain useful even when you use a local model or a non-AI baseline instead.

title: Preface
text:
A note on responsible use
AI outputs can be plausible and wrong. They can omit important context, reflect bias in the data or evaluation, and reveal information when data handling is poorly designed. A prototype should therefore state what information it uses, what it is allowed to do, how its outputs are checked, and when a human must decide.
Pay particular attention to tasks involving health, finance, legal matters, employment, education, or personal data. In those settings, examples in this guide are learning exercises, and deployment requires domain-specific review, appropriate safeguards, and stronger evidence than a classroom prototype provides.

title: Preface
text:
Before continuing
Choose one potential task and write a short problem statement:

For [specific user], given [permitted input], the prototype will produce [defined output] to help with [specific task]. We will judge it using [representative examples and criteria], and a person will review [cases needing oversight].

You may revise this statement as you learn. A narrow first version makes the eventual prototype easier to build and evaluate.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: Begin with a task people need to complete
text:
Begin with a task people need to complete
“Build an AI assistant” describes a technology choice. It does not explain whose work should improve, what information the assistant may use, or how anyone will know that it helps.
Consider a training centre whose staff repeatedly answer questions about course registration. One proposal is to build a chatbot. A better starting point is to observe the work: staff find the relevant policy, check that it applies to the question, and explain the answer. Sometimes the published information is incomplete, and staff must refer the question to a coordinator.
That observation suggests a bounded first task:

Help a course administrator locate the approved passage that answers a registration question, or identify that the question needs further review.

A searchable page might solve this task. A retrieval system might improve it. A language model might help draft an explanation after retrieval. The task determines what to compare; the technology does not define success.
The prototype in this chapter uses fictional course policies and synthetic questions. It illustrates problem framing and evaluation without using personal data, contacting an AI service, or making claims about a trained model’s performance.
This course-policy task is the running example in the first chapters. It gives us a small document collection, observable errors, and a baseline that we can inspect. Later, we will transfer the same questions about source quality, evaluation, and human review to CDI research data, where the source documents and consequences differ.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: What makes a system an AI system?
text:
What makes a system an AI system?
AI is a broad field concerned with systems that perform tasks such as perception, language processing, reasoning, prediction, and planning. The OECD’s explanatory memorandum describes AI systems in terms of how they infer outputs from inputs; those outputs can include predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions. The definition accommodates different levels of autonomy and does not require a conversational interface (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development 2024).
For this guide, four terms are useful:








Term
Practical meaning
Example




Artificial intelligence
The wider field of systems performing tasks associated with intelligent behaviour
A system that interprets a question and proposes an answer


Machine learning
Methods that estimate patterns from data
A classifier learned from labelled support requests


Deep learning
Machine learning using multilayer neural networks
A neural model that represents text or images


Generative AI
Systems that produce content such as text, images, or audio
A model drafting an explanation from retrieved passages



These terms overlap. Generative AI is not synonymous with all AI, and not every useful automation requires machine learning. Modern generative systems commonly use deep learning, but this chapter does not require training or running one.

A model is one component of an application
A model transforms inputs into outputs. An application also has data access, interfaces, rules, error handling, review procedures, and people who act on its outputs.
For the course administrator, a fluent response is insufficient if it cites an outdated policy. A good model can still be part of an unreliable application when the wrong document is retrieved, the user cannot inspect the source, or an answer is sent without the necessary review.
Think of the complete workflow:

User need → bounded task → permitted information → method → checked output → action → feedback

Each transition deserves a question. Is the input in scope? Is the information current? Does the evidence support the output? Can the user correct an error? What happens when the system cannot answer?

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: Define the problem before selecting an approach
text:
Define the problem before selecting an approach
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework emphasizes understanding intended purposes, context, and relevant stakeholders, and evaluating systems in their intended settings (Tabassi 2023). This chapter turns that general principle into a practical brief; the worksheet is a teaching aid, not a certification checklist.

User and affected people
Name the person who will use the output, and distinguish them from people affected by it. Here, the direct user is a course administrator; prospective learners are affected by any information they receive.
“Everyone” is rarely a useful first audience. A narrow audience makes vocabulary, accessibility, working conditions, and review responsibilities easier to specify.


Task and unit of work
Describe one instance of work. In the running example, the unit is one registration question checked against one approved policy collection.
Avoid combining unrelated tasks into the first version. Answering policy questions, deciding admission, collecting payments, and predicting dropout are separate tasks with different evidence and consequences.


Permitted inputs and knowledge boundary
Specify what the system receives and what it may consult. The example accepts a short English question and searches four fictional policy passages. It has no access to learner records, private messages, or live course availability.
An input boundary prevents hidden assumptions. If a question needs information outside the approved collection, the correct behaviour is to refer it for review. Adding a powerful model would not create missing institutional knowledge.


Output contract
An output contract states what an acceptable result contains. Our baseline returns:

the original question identifier;
either a policy identifier or REVIEW;
the selected policy passage, if any; and
a status explaining whether there was one rule match, no match, or conflicting matches.

The first version returns source text rather than a generated paraphrase. This makes the evidence inspectable. A later draft-answer feature would need additional criteria for factual support, completeness, and misleading wording.


Action and authority
The administrator reads the result, checks the passage, and decides how to respond. The prototype does not send messages, change enrolments, grant exceptions, or make decisions about eligibility.
“Human review” must identify a real step. Specify who checks what, what evidence they see, and whether they have time and authority to reject the output. A nominal reviewer who accepts every result is not a demonstrated safeguard.


Constraints and failure consequences
Record constraints that could change the design: language, connectivity, response time, approved data sources, privacy, accessibility, and maintenance responsibilities.
For this task, a wrong policy citation could mislead a learner; unnecessary referral costs staff time. These errors are not equivalent. A design that refers uncertain cases can be useful even if it answers fewer questions automatically, provided that referral is reliable and staff capacity is adequate.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
text:
Write a one-page problem brief
Use this sentence as the starting point:

For [user], given [permitted input], produce [defined output] to support [task or action]. Compare against [baseline] using [representative cases and criteria]. Refer [conditions] to [responsible person], within [constraints].

A completed version for the example is:

For course administrators, given a short registration question and an approved policy collection, return a relevant passage or a review flag so staff can prepare a supported response. Compare candidate approaches with keyword routing on policy questions, paraphrases, multi-topic requests, and questions outside the collection. Measure correct routing, incorrect automatic routing, and review volume. Staff check every result; admission decisions and personal records remain outside scope.

The included data/reference/01-problem-brief-template.md expands this into a reusable worksheet. Keep the brief short enough to review with the intended user. Where evidence is missing, write “to be measured” rather than inventing a success claim.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: Match the approach to the task
text:
Match the approach to the task








Approach
Appropriate starting condition
Main limitation to examine




Explicit rule or lookup
Stable, clearly stated conditions map to known outputs
Brittle wording and incomplete rules


Search or retrieval
Answers already exist in an approved collection
Failure to retrieve the right, current source


Supervised prediction
Relevant examples have reliable target labels
Generalization, label quality, and data leakage


Generative model
The task needs flexible drafting or transformation
Unsupported, incomplete, or inconsistent content


Retrieval with generation
A draft must use an identifiable knowledge collection
Retrieval errors and unsupported synthesis


Human process
Judgment or missing context dominates the task
Capacity, consistency, and turnaround time



These are starting points, not mutually exclusive categories. A workflow can combine search, rules, and a model. Retrieval does not guarantee that a generated answer is correct, and adding a model does not automatically improve a deterministic task.

When to narrow or stop
Pause the prototype if there is no agreed task, no usable evidence for checking outputs, no permitted information source, or no owner for consequential errors. Also reconsider AI when a maintained FAQ or existing search interface already meets the need.
A useful first experiment should resolve a specific uncertainty: for example, whether paraphrased questions can be matched to the right policy. “Explore what AI can do” is too broad to provide a clear stopping condition.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: Design the evaluation before improving the method
text:
Design the evaluation before improving the method
A baseline is a reference method against which a new approach is compared. It might be the current manual workflow, a majority prediction, a keyword rule, or ordinary search. Its purpose is to establish what improvement means.
Use the same evaluation cases and output requirements when comparing approaches. If one method may consult extra documents or gets easier questions, a higher score does not isolate the value of the method.

Cases should reflect the intended work
Include routine cases and cases that test boundaries:

direct questions that use policy vocabulary;
paraphrases that avoid expected keywords;
questions covering multiple topics;
questions with missing context;
questions outside the approved collection; and
supported languages and accessibility needs relevant to the real setting.

A small synthetic set is useful for debugging the workflow. It cannot establish population-level reliability, fairness, or production readiness. Later evaluation should use independently labelled, representative cases obtained through appropriate data handling.
Keep development cases separate from final evaluation cases. Once you use a case to revise rules or prompts, it becomes part of development. Repeatedly improving against the same small set creates an optimistic estimate of performance.


Define metrics with denominators
For our routing task, use three quantities:
\[
\text{Correct routing rate} = \frac{\text{cases matching the expected route}}{\text{all cases}}.
\]
An expected route may be a policy identifier or REVIEW. Correct referral therefore counts as correct routing.
\[
\text{Incorrect automatic routing rate} = \frac{\text{wrong policy routes}}{\text{all automatic policy routes}}.
\]
\[
\text{Review rate} = \frac{\text{cases sent to review}}{\text{all cases}}.
\]
The second metric is undefined when there are no automatic routes; the script reports NA in that situation. Always show counts with rates. The denominator affects interpretation: a method that refers every question has no incorrect automatic routes, but may offer no time saving.


Turn aspirations into acceptance criteria
“Accurate and fast” does not define an acceptance test. A prototype brief could instead say:

every automatic result includes an inspectable approved passage;
no case deliberately labelled outside scope receives an automatic policy route in the development suite;
multi-topic requests are referred under the agreed single-passage contract; and
a staff pilot measures correction time and referral workload before claiming time savings.

These are example development criteria, not universal performance thresholds. A real team must agree on error tolerances, sample sizes, service requirements, and escalation arrangements for its own setting.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
section: Worked example: evaluate a transparent baseline
text:
Worked example: evaluate a transparent baseline
The chapter’s runnable example is a deterministic keyword router. It is intentionally simple so that every result can be traced to a rule. It does not train an AI model. It gives a later AI approach a concrete baseline to improve upon.
Four fictional policies cover registration, certificates, refunds, and course schedules. The synthetic test set contains 16 questions: four direct questions, four paraphrases, four multi-topic requests, and four questions outside the collection.
The script searches whole words in each question. One matching policy returns its passage; no matches or several policy matches return REVIEW.
matches = [
    policy_id
    for policy_id, policy in policies.items()
    if tokens.intersection(policy["keywords"])
]
route = matches[0] if len(matches) == 1 else "REVIEW"
This displayed fragment is illustrative. The complete program is in scripts/python/01-ai-problem-framing.py. Plain code fences do not execute during Quarto rendering.

Run the example
Use the Artificial Intelligence repository’s own .venv, as described in the preface. The program uses the Python standard library and Matplotlib; Matplotlib is already listed in the guide’s requirements.txt.
From the repository root, install the documented dependencies if needed, then run:
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
bash scripts/bash/01-ai-problem-framing.sh
The wrapper uses .venv/bin/python explicitly and stops with a useful message if the environment is missing. Alternatively, invoke the Python program directly with that interpreter:
.venv/bin/python scripts/python/01-ai-problem-framing.py
The program resolves paths from its own file location. It therefore writes to the intended repository even when called from a different working directory. No API key, network request, random seed, or downloaded dataset is needed: all input cases and rules are fixed and versionable. The inputs are fictional policies in data/reference/01-course-policies.json and 16 synthetic, labelled questions in data/reference/01-framing-cases.csv; they are not empirical observations. The reusable worksheet is data/reference/01-problem-brief-template.md.


Inspect the outputs







File
Purpose




results/tables/01-routing-results.csv
Every question, expected route, actual route, passage, and error flags


results/tables/01-routing-summary.csv
Counts and rates overall and by case family


results/figures/01-ai-task-workflow.png
The bounded task and its human decision point


results/figures/01-baseline-routing-results.png
Correct routes, unnecessary reviews, and wrong automatic routes


results/tables/01-run-metadata.json
Runtime versions and input hashes for tracing the run









Figure 1.1: The workflow takes a question and approved policies, routes to a passage or review, and requires an administrator to check the result before responding.



Figure 1.1 makes the boundary visible: retrieving a passage supports the administrator’s work, while the response remains a human action.






Figure 1.2: A stacked bar chart compares routing outcomes across four synthetic question families.





Interpret the result
The fixed example produces:








Quantity
Result
Interpretation




Correct routes
10 / 16 (62.5%)
Includes six correct referrals and four correct policy routes


Automatic policy routes
6 / 16 (37.5%)
Four are correct; two are wrong


Incorrect automatic routing rate
2 / 6 (33.3%)
One third of automatic routes fail on this tiny set


Review rate
10 / 16 (62.5%)
Six reviews are expected; four are avoidable misses



The aggregate correct-routing rate hides two different failures. The router misses all four paraphrases because they avoid its keywords. It also routes “birth certificate” and “bus schedule” questions to course policies because isolated keywords do not establish meaning.
The two wrong automatic routes violate the example development criterion for outside-scope questions. The baseline is therefore useful as an experiment, but it does not meet that criterion.
The chart uses counts rather than percentages because each family contains only four cases. The dataset was constructed to illustrate failure modes; the family frequencies do not represent actual demand. Do not interpret the 33.3% result as a forecast of real-world error. The outputs are reproducible from the supplied source and inputs, and the run metadata records runtime versions and SHA-256 hashes. Inspect the CSVs if you need the case-level counts behind the table.


Decide what the evidence supports
This run supports a limited conclusion: keyword overlap alone cannot reliably distinguish the intended questions in this test set. It does not prove that a language model will solve the problem.
Possible next experiments include improving ordinary search, introducing explicit topic disambiguation, or comparing semantic retrieval on a separate set of questions. A generated draft would require additional evaluation of factual support and wording. Record the reason for each change and preserve the baseline outputs.
The REVIEW route also needs care. It groups ambiguous questions, missing coverage, and unmatched wording under one operational action. A later version might distinguish these causes to help staff resolve them, but only if the extra categories improve the workflow.

title: AI Thinking and Problem Framing
text:
Common framing mistakes








Mistake
Why it weakens the project
Better framing




“Use the strongest model”
Names a component without defining value
Specify the task and compare measured outcomes


“Answer any question”
Hides the knowledge and authority boundaries
Name approved sources and referral conditions


“The answer sounds right”
Fluency is not evidence of support
Check it against an agreed source and rubric


“A person will review it”
Omits the reviewer’s actual work
Specify evidence, time, authority, and escalation


“It scored well on our examples”
Development cases can overstate reliability
Reserve independent evaluation cases


“It will save staff time”
Omits checking and correction costs
Measure the complete task, including rework



A predictive association also does not establish the effect of an intervention. If a later model predicts which learners may disengage, that prediction alone does not show which support action will help them. The intervention question needs its own evidence and study design.

Check your understanding

Why is “build a course chatbot” less useful than a bounded problem statement?
Why can a system that sends every case to review avoid wrong automatic routes without improving the workflow?
Does returning a correct passage prove that a generated answer based on it would be correct?
Which example result shows that a keyword can match while the question remains outside scope?







Suggested answers






It leaves the user, permitted sources, output, action, and success criteria unspecified.
It transfers all work to staff. Review capacity and total task time must also be measured; the wrong-automatic-route rate has no denominator when there are no automatic routes.
No. Generation can omit a condition, misstate the passage, or add unsupported claims. Retrieval and answer quality require separate checks.
The birth-certificate and bus-schedule questions match course-policy keywords but request information absent from the collection.

Try it yourself: produce a reviewable problem brief
Choose a modest task from your own work: locating an approved procedure, routing support questions, or extracting fields from a standard form.

Complete data/reference/01-problem-brief-template.md in a separate copy.
Define the output contract and at least three conditions requiring review.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
From a task to a system
Chapter 01 began with a user and a defined task. Before choosing an AI tool, we need to understand what information the system will receive, what the model can do with it, and how an output is produced.
Consider the proposed research paper assistant. A reviewer supplies an approved article and requests four fields: aim, methods, findings, and limitations. A model might produce a fluent summary, but the reviewer needs something more specific: claims supported by the article, traceable references, and a clear signal when the article does not provide an answer.
Three terms help us reason about this workflow:
These definitions are related but distinct. Supplying a new article to an existing model is inference; it does not usually retrain the model. Editing a prompt changes what we ask the model to do, not the learned parameters inside it.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
Data are the information used to develop, configure, supply, and assess the system.
A model is a learned mechanism that maps an input to a prediction, representation, or generated output.
Inference is the act of using a trained model on a particular input to produce an output.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
The different roles of data
“The data” can refer to several different things. Keeping them separate prevents mistakes in design and evaluation.








Data role
Example in the article task
Main question




Development examples
A small set of articles used to refine instructions
Are examples varied enough to reveal common failures?


Input at use time
The article a reviewer currently supplies
Is its text complete, permitted, and readable?


Reference material
Passages retrieved from the article for a particular question
Can each passage be traced to its source?


Evaluation cases
Articles and expected behaviors reserved for assessment
Do they represent the intended use and difficult cases?


Feedback
Reviewer corrections and error notes
Can they be recorded and used appropriately?



A model may also have been trained on a large collection of data before you obtain access to it. You generally cannot assume that its training material includes your specific article, is current, or is authoritative for your task. Supply relevant approved source information at use time when the answer must depend on that source, and still verify the resulting claims.

Data quality is task specific
Useful data must be appropriate for the decision the system supports. In the article example, important properties include:

Completeness: Are pages, tables, and appendices available when they matter?
Readability: Was text extracted accurately, including headings and numbers?
Provenance: Which article and section supplied a passage?
Relevance: Does the supplied article actually address the requested question?
Permission: May the document be processed with the chosen tool?
Representativeness: Do evaluation articles reflect the formats and topics users will encounter?

A large collection does not compensate for missing methods sections, corrupted tables, or evaluation examples that avoid difficult cases.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
What a model learns
A model is built by adjusting internal parameters using examples and an objective. Different model families learn different relationships. A classifier might estimate which label fits an input; a language model predicts or generates sequences of text. Later chapters introduce machine learning, neural networks, language models, and image systems in more detail.
Training, selection, and use should not be treated as the same operation:

Training adjusts model parameters from training data.
Selection or configuration chooses a model, prompt, settings, or supporting workflow for a task.
Inference applies the configured system to a new input.
Evaluation compares its behavior with criteria and examples that reflect the intended task.

Some systems include additional learned components, such as a text extraction model or a retrieval model. The output of the complete workflow depends on all of them, not only the final language model.

A model is not a source of record
A fluent answer may combine useful patterns with unsupported claims. Model confidence expressed in natural language is not evidence that a statement is correct. For source-based work, the article remains the source of record. The output must be checked against it.
This distinction also applies to general knowledge questions. A model can help formulate an answer, but a consequential or time-sensitive claim should be checked against an appropriate source.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
What happens during inference
At inference time, the system receives an input and produces an output. For a document assistant, the real sequence may be:

Receive the approved document and the user’s request.
Extract readable text and preserve page or section references.
Select relevant passages if the document is too large or the task is focused.
Provide instructions and selected material to the model.
Receive a draft and validate its expected structure.
Present the draft and supporting passages to a human reviewer.

Each step can fail. A missing page can lead to an omitted limitation. Poor passage selection can hide a qualifying sentence. A structured draft can still contain an unsupported claim. Human review is therefore part of the designed workflow, not a substitute for evaluating it.

Inputs, parameters, and outputs
An AI result depends on more than the words typed into a prompt:








Element
Example
Why record it?




Input
Article version and user request
Different inputs can produce different answers


Model
Provider, model identifier, and available version
Behavior may vary by model or version


Instructions
Task definition and output requirements
Small changes can change the answer


Context
Supplied or retrieved passages
Missing or irrelevant context changes what is supported


Settings
Applicable generation settings
They can affect variation and output length


Postprocessing
Parsing and checks
A valid format does not guarantee factual correctness



Recording these elements helps reproduce and investigate an output. Chapter 11 develops reproducible AI workflows more fully.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
section: Three ways information can reach a model
text:
Three ways information can reach a model
The distinction below is especially useful when planning a prototype:








Method
What changes?
Suitable question




Prompt or instructions
The request sent at inference time
Can we specify the task more clearly?


Supplied or retrieved context
The information available for this request
Can the answer be grounded in an approved source?


Additional training or fine-tuning
Some learned parameters or model behavior
Do we have evidence that a trained adaptation is needed?



These methods solve different problems. Supplying article passages can help a model answer from that article, but it does not guarantee that the model uses them correctly. Fine-tuning a model does not automatically make it a reliable store of current document facts. Start with the task and the observed failure before deciding which intervention to try.

title: Data, Models, and Inference
text:
Data leakage and evaluation boundaries
An evaluation case should reveal how the system performs on examples it has not been optimized to answer. If you repeatedly inspect an evaluation article while revising the prompt, it becomes part of development. Set aside other cases for a more independent check.
Leakage can also arise when an input contains information that would be unavailable in real use. For example, a triage assistant evaluated with notes written after a case was resolved may appear unusually accurate. Chapter 01’s question—what is available at the time of use?—protects the evaluation as well as the prototype.
For generative tasks, a single reference answer may be too restrictive because several summaries can be valid. Evaluate required facts, supporting evidence, omissions, and unacceptable errors as well as any agreement with a reference draft.

text:
Looking ahead
Chapter 03 places these ideas in context by explaining how artificial intelligence and machine learning relate, which problems learned models address, and when a non-learning method is sufficient.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Where machine learning fits
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad field concerned with systems that perform tasks associated with perception, reasoning, language, planning, or decision-making. The OECD’s updated definition describes AI systems in terms of how they infer outputs, including predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions, from their inputs (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development 2024). Machine learning (ML) is one way to build such systems: a model learns useful patterns from examples rather than having every possible case specified by hand.
Not every AI system is a machine-learning model. A system can combine fixed rules, search, a knowledge base, and a learned model. Nor does every task that sounds “intelligent” require AI. If a clearly defined rule solves the user’s problem, the rule may be the better choice.
The terms are related as follows:
These are overlapping descriptions of methods and capabilities, not a ladder of quality. A generative system may use deep learning; a broader AI workflow may also include ordinary software and human review. The right method depends on the task and evidence, not on which term sounds more advanced.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Term
Working meaning
Example




Artificial intelligence
Broad area of systems performing tasks that require context-sensitive interpretation or action
An assistant that finds and summarizes permitted documents


Machine learning
Methods that learn relationships from examples
A classifier trained to label incoming requests


Deep learning
Machine learning using multilayer neural networks
A model that recognizes patterns in images or text


Generative AI
Models that generate content such as text, images, or audio
A language model drafting a summary

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Rules and learned patterns
Suppose a research assistant must identify the publication year of an article. If that year is in a reliable metadata field, a direct lookup is straightforward. If article files vary and metadata are missing, extraction may require more flexible text processing. If the task is to interpret a study’s limitations, rules alone may struggle with the variety of wording and context.









Approach
How it handles a new case
Typical strength
Typical limitation




Fixed rule
Applies instructions written in advance
Predictable for well-defined cases
Brittle when inputs vary beyond the rules


Search or retrieval
Finds matching records or passages
Traceable to source material
Finding a passage does not interpret it


Trained predictive model
Uses learned relationships to estimate an outcome
Handles patterns across many examples
Depends on suitable training data and evaluation


Generative model
Produces content conditioned on an input and instructions
Flexible drafting and transformation
Can produce fluent but unsupported content


Human-led workflow
Applies domain judgment and accountability
Handles ambiguity and consequences
Requires time and may vary across reviewers



Real applications often combine approaches. A document assistant could use search to locate passages, a language model to draft a summary, fixed checks to ensure required fields are present, and a reviewer to verify meaning. The chosen design and level of review should reflect the system’s context and risks; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a structured approach to considering those risks (Tabassi 2023).

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Common machine-learning tasks
The task describes the expected output. It does not by itself specify which algorithm to use.

Classification
Classification assigns one or more categories to an input. An example is labeling a support message as a billing question, an access problem, or another request. The categories must be defined clearly, and some messages may belong to more than one category or none of the planned categories.


Regression
Regression estimates a numeric value, such as the expected number of days to complete a process. Its accuracy depends on what information is available when the estimate is made and whether past examples reflect future cases.


Ranking
Ranking orders candidates, such as documents likely to be relevant to a search. The first result may matter more than the tenth, so evaluation should reflect how people use the ordered list.


Clustering
Clustering groups examples by similarity without requiring predefined labels for every group. A cluster is a pattern in the available representation, not automatically a meaningful real-world category. People must inspect and interpret the groups.


Generation
Generation produces new text, images, or other content conditioned on a request. A paper summary is a generation task, but it also requires factual support and may depend on retrieval. Evaluating only whether the prose reads well would miss the core requirement.
The same user need can contain several tasks. A literature assistant might rank papers, extract study characteristics, and generate a reviewer-facing draft. Define and evaluate each step rather than giving the entire workflow one vague “accuracy” score.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
How learning from examples differs
There are several ways models can learn. The distinctions help you understand the resources and evaluation each approach needs.








Learning setup
Available signal
Illustrative use




Supervised learning
Inputs paired with target labels or values
Predict a defined request category from past labeled requests


Unsupervised learning
Inputs without task-specific target labels
Explore groups of similar documents


Self-supervised learning
Training signals derived from the data itself
Learn general representations from text or images



These labels describe training setups. They do not guarantee an appropriate model, trustworthy data, or useful performance on your particular task. A general-purpose language model may have learned broad patterns before you use it, while your application still needs task-specific instructions, source material, and evaluation.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
General models and task-specific systems
A model can provide a capability without constituting a complete solution. For example, a language model may write a plausible summary. A dependable article-summary workflow additionally needs document intake, text extraction, source references, output formatting, verification, and review.
Distinguish three levels:

Model capability: Can the model perform a type of transformation at all?
Task performance: Does it do so on representative examples under the stated constraints?
Workflow usefulness: Does the full process improve the user’s work after corrections, delays, and costs are counted?

A good demonstration at level one does not establish levels two and three. This is why the problem brief from Chapter 01 and the data map from Chapter 02 come before choosing a model.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Continue the article example
Our defined task is to draft four article-summary fields, each supported by a section reference, for review. Several approaches are possible:








Candidate
How it would work
What to test




Manual template
Reviewer reads and fills four fields
Time, consistency, and errors in the current workflow


Search plus template
Reviewer uses section search and fills fields
Whether search reduces effort without hiding context


Language-model draft
Model receives the article and instructions
Support, omissions, corrections, and reviewer time


Retrieval plus draft
Relevant passages are selected before generation
Whether selection improves support or omits key context



The manual or search-assisted workflow is a meaningful baseline. If the model saves drafting time but takes longer to verify, the benefit may disappear. If retrieval excludes the limitations section, a fluent generated answer may perform worse than a simple template.
The choice is therefore a hypothesis:

For approved articles in scope, a model-assisted draft with traceable references will reduce reviewer effort while meeting the agreed support and accuracy criteria.

The hypothesis can be rejected. That is a useful outcome: it prevents investing further in a method that does not help the user.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Avoid three common shortcuts

Choosing a model before defining the task
Starting with a popular model encourages a demonstration designed around its strengths. Start with the user’s work, constraints, and baseline; then compare tools that could meet those needs.


Equating training success with real use
Performance on training examples does not show how a model handles unfamiliar documents, changed wording, or missing information. Reserve appropriate evaluation cases and measure the workflow under conditions resembling use.


Treating generation as understanding
Well-formed text can be wrong or unsupported. Require source checks, explicit uncertainty, and human review where errors matter. Do not infer factual reliability from a polished writing style.

title: AI and Machine Learning
text:
Practice: justify an approach
Return to your problem brief and data-and-inference map:

State the primary task: classification, numeric prediction, ranking, grouping, generation, or a combination.
Identify one non-ML baseline that could address all or part of it.
Identify one learned approach and the data or context it would require.
Compare likely failure modes, verification effort, cost, and permissions.
Write a testable hypothesis explaining why the learned approach might help.
State what finding would lead you to retain the simpler baseline.

For a multi-step workflow, repeat the exercise for each step. You may discover that only one component benefits from a learned model.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Why this chapter matters
Chapter 03 compared rules, retrieval, predictive models, and generation. Many modern systems used for language, images, and audio rely on neural networks. To select one responsibly, you need a working account of what the model learns, what happens when it receives a new input, and why a capable general model can still fail at your particular task.
You do not need to train a large network for the article-summary prototype. Understanding the mechanism will help you decide whether an existing model is useful, what evidence to request, and where checks belong in the workflow.

title: Neural Networks
text:
From inputs to outputs
A neural network is a model with adjustable numerical parameters. It transforms an input through a sequence of operations to produce an output. During training, examples guide changes to those parameters so that the model performs better according to a chosen objective.
For a simple network, one layer can be written as:
\[
\mathbf{h}=g(W\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}),
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}\) is a numerical representation of the input, \(W\) contains learned weights, \(\mathbf{b}\) contains learned offsets, and \(g\) is a nonlinear activation function. The resulting values \(\mathbf{h}\) become input to another layer or an output calculation. The word neuron is a convenient analogy for a small computation; it does not mean the system thinks like a person.
A network used to classify messages could turn text into numerical representations, combine those representations through learned layers, and return scores for categories. A language model instead uses its context to produce a distribution over possible next tokens, generating a response one token at a time. The task, architecture, data, and training objective determine what the output means.

title: Neural Networks
text:
What training changes
A typical training loop has four stages:

Forward pass: compute an output for an example or batch.
Loss: compare the output with the training objective using a numerical measure of error.
Gradient calculation: estimate how changes to the parameters would affect that loss, commonly using backpropagation.
Update: adjust parameters with an optimization method and repeat across examples.

The network learns parameter values that improve its training objective. That achievement does not establish that an answer is true, that an explanation is faithful, or that the system will work on new users’ documents. Those are separate questions for evaluation.
Training a model from scratch requires data, compute, and careful validation. A small prototype will often use an existing model through an approved local or hosted interface. You still need to test the complete workflow on representative inputs.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Learned representations
A useful feature of layered models is that intermediate values can represent patterns that were not specified as individual rules. In image tasks, these may support recognition of visual structures. In language tasks, they can encode relationships among tokens and surrounding context. The representation depends on the model and training data; an apparently meaningful pattern need not match the user’s intended concept.
Compare two approaches to locating an article’s limitations:








Approach
Possible strength
Possible failure




Search for a heading or keyword
Easy to inspect and trace
Misses an unusual heading or wording


Neural language model
Can handle varied phrasing and context
May infer a limitation the article never states


Search followed by model-assisted extraction
Grounds the draft in selected passages
Retrieval may exclude a relevant passage



These methods can work together. The network adds flexibility, while the source passage and reviewer provide checks on what it produces.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Training, adaptation, and inference
Keep three activities distinct:

Pretraining develops broad capability from a large collection of examples using a general training objective.
Task adaptation may use additional training or other configuration to improve performance on a narrower task. Instructions and retrieved documents can also shape behavior at use time without changing model weights.
Inference applies the already trained model to a new input. A normal prompt changes the context supplied for that request; it does not retrain the model.

A general language model may draft clear summaries without knowing what your reviewer considers an acceptable article-summary field. Giving it an approved article and a precise instruction can help. Neither step alone proves that every field is supported.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Generalization and its limits
The useful question is whether a network performs well on cases it did not learn or tune against. A model can appear strong on familiar examples yet struggle with different document layouts, technical vocabulary, long articles, scanned pages, or articles that do not report the requested field.
For the article-summary workflow, set aside articles representing these differences. Include cases where the answer is genuinely absent. Check whether the draft reports that absence instead of filling the gap with plausible language. Keep evaluation cases separate from examples repeatedly used to edit a prompt.
The same principle applies to smaller supervised networks: a low training loss does not replace evaluation on independent data. Model size and fluent output are not measures of fitness for a specific task.

title: Neural Networks
section: A closer look at language models
text:
A closer look at language models
Modern language models commonly use transformer architectures that process token representations in context. An attention mechanism allows parts of the input to influence other parts as the model constructs its representations. This helps the model use surrounding text, but attention is not a guarantee that it identified the decisive evidence or that its generated answer follows from that evidence.
Language models work with tokens, which can be words, word parts, punctuation, or other units depending on the tokenizer. An article and its instructions must fit within the model’s usable context for a request. Even when a document fits, important details can be missed. If the application supplies selected passages instead, selection quality becomes another part of the system to evaluate. Chapter 05 develops language models and generation in more detail; Chapter 08 examines retrieval and tools.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Continue the article-summary example
Suppose the prototype asks for four fields: study aim, study design, main finding, and stated limitations. Each field must cite a section or passage from the supplied article. The model may draft the fields, but the workflow should define what to do when a passage is missing or ambiguous.








Component
Role
Check




Approved article text
Supplies permitted source material
Confirm article identity and readable extraction


Instructions
Define fields, format, and absence handling
Inspect whether the request matches the reviewer’s task


Existing language model
Drafts candidate fields
Evaluate support, omissions, and incorrect claims


Passage references
Let a reviewer inspect the basis for each field
Verify that each reference exists and supports its claim


Human reviewer
Accepts, corrects, or rejects the draft
Record corrections and time spent



A passage reference generated by a model is only a claim about support. The reviewer or an independent check must confirm it. If the source does not state a limitation, the appropriate draft may be “not stated in the supplied article,” with that absence flagged for review.

title: Neural Networks
section: Decide whether a neural network is warranted
text:
Decide whether a neural network is warranted
Use the candidate method from Chapter 03 and ask:

Does the task require flexible interpretation of varied text, images, or other complex inputs?
Can a rule, search, or template meet the same need with acceptable effort?
Are the necessary inputs permitted, legible, and representative?
Can each important output be checked against a source or other reference?
What happens when the model is uncertain, the input is outside scope, or the source lacks an answer?
Does the full workflow improve accuracy or reviewer effort after corrections, cost, and delay are included?

A neural model is suitable when its measured benefit justifies its added complexity for this task. The comparison is a practical test, not a declaration that one family of methods is universally superior.

title: Neural Networks
text:
Practice: write a suitability note
For your own proposed prototype, write six short statements:

Input: What will the network receive, and where does it come from?
Output: What exactly should it produce?
Reason to try it: Which variation or complexity is difficult for the baseline?
Baseline: What simpler process will you compare it with?
Evidence: Which held-out cases and checks would demonstrate improvement?
Boundary: Which output must a person verify, and when should the system abstain?

For the article example, the note might say: “We will test whether a language-model draft reduces reviewer time for four supported fields on approved articles. We will compare it with a manual template using reserved articles, check each cited passage, count omissions and unsupported claims, and require a reviewer to approve the final summary.”

title: Language Models and Generative AI
text:
From neural networks to generated content
Chapter 04 explained how neural networks learn adjustable representations and why fluent output needs independent checks. This chapter focuses on language models: systems that use a text context to generate or transform text. They can draft, summarize, extract, classify, translate, and help organize information. Their flexibility makes them useful in a prototype, but the same flexibility makes the boundaries of a task important.
For the continuing example, a reviewer wants a draft with four fields about an approved research article: study aim, study design, main finding, and stated limitations. Each field needs a passage reference. The goal is to help the reviewer inspect and complete the summary, not to let fluent prose substitute for the article.

title: Language Models and Generative AI
section: What a language model receives and produces
text:
What a language model receives and produces
A language model receives a sequence of tokens representing its available context. Tokens may correspond to whole words, pieces of words, punctuation, or other units. The context can include instructions, a user request, examples, and source text supplied for the current request.
The model assigns relative likelihoods to possible next tokens and selects one according to its generation settings. The selected token joins the context, and the process repeats. This explains how a response can be coherent without being a checked account of the world. A high likelihood for a continuation means that it fits the model’s learned patterns and current context; it does not establish that the statement is supported by the article.
Many practical applications wrap this model behavior in other components: document extraction, retrieval, output validation, access controls, and human review. Evaluate the resulting workflow as well as the model’s individual response.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
section: Generative AI is broader than chat
text:
Generative AI is broader than chat
Generative models can produce or transform text, images, audio, video, code, and structured content. A language model may also help with tasks whose desired output is short and constrained, such as assigning a category or filling fields. In those cases, generation is the mechanism, while the user’s task is classification or extraction.








User task
Requested output
Main test




Drafting
A proposed paragraph or message
Does it meet the brief and preserve the intended meaning?


Summarization
A shorter account of source material
Are the important claims supported and key qualifications retained?


Extraction
Named facts or fields from a source
Are values copied or paraphrased correctly, with missing items marked?


Classification
A label from a defined set
Does the label match reviewed examples and decision rules?


Question answering
A response to a specific question
Is the answer supported by permitted evidence, or does it abstain?



The same model can attempt all five. Each task needs its own criteria, baseline, and examples. A pleasant writing style is useful for drafting but cannot replace a source-support test for extraction or question answering.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
section: The difference between training knowledge and supplied evidence
text:
The difference between training knowledge and supplied evidence
A model may have learned broad patterns during training. It may therefore explain a common concept without receiving a source document. That does not mean it has access to your current article, a complete and authoritative record, or the exact passage behind a claim.
For a document-specific task, give the system the approved source material through a deliberate workflow. Ask it to identify where each claim comes from and then verify the references. Source text in a prompt, a retrieved passage, or an uploaded document is context supplied for this request; it does not automatically become permanent training data for the model. Data handling depends on the chosen service and configuration and must be checked for the actual project.
If the article is absent, unreadable, incomplete, or outside the model’s available context, the system should identify that limitation. It should not reconstruct a plausible study from a title or its general knowledge.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
section: Why generated answers can be wrong
text:
Why generated answers can be wrong
A model can produce a statement that sounds reasonable but is unsupported, misquoted, or false. This may occur when the requested information is missing, the input is ambiguous, the source text was extracted badly, or the prompt encourages an answer despite uncertainty. Generation settings alone cannot guarantee accuracy.
For the article summary, inspect several distinct error types:

Invented content: a study result or limitation absent from the article.
Misattribution: a real statement assigned to the wrong section or study.
Lost qualification: “may be associated with” rewritten as “causes.”
Omission: a major limitation or relevant condition left out.
Unsupported reference: a cited passage exists but does not justify the field.
False completeness: a missing field is filled with a guess instead of marked for review.

These errors have different remedies. Clearer instructions may help with a format failure. Better source extraction or retrieval may help with missing evidence. Human review may remain necessary for subtle interpretations. Chapter 09 develops a systematic evaluation and failure-analysis process.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
text:
Context is useful but finite
Models can use a limited amount of text in a single request. The exact limit and behavior depend on the selected system. A long article, appendices, instructions, and examples may compete for available space. Even when text is accepted, the model can overlook an important passage or confuse nearby details.
For short articles, the complete text may be manageable. For larger collections, a retrieval step can select candidate passages before generation. That introduces a new question: did retrieval find all material needed to answer? A model cannot faithfully summarize an omitted section it never received. Chapter 08 examines retrieval and tools as parts of the workflow.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
section: Control the task, then check the result
text:
Control the task, then check the result
A useful request defines the task and the expected behavior for gaps. For example:

Using only the supplied article text, draft the study aim, study design, main finding, and stated limitations. For each field, include a short section or passage reference. If a field is not supported by the supplied text, write “not established in supplied text.” Do not infer missing results. Return the four fields separately for reviewer verification.

This instruction narrows the task. It does not enforce truth. The prototype must still verify whether the stated references exist and support the draft. Later chapters cover prompting, structured outputs, and evaluation in more detail.
Distinguish format checks from content checks. A program can verify that four fields are present and that each has a reference field. A reviewer or source-aware evaluation must determine whether the cited passage actually supports the claim.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
text:
Generation settings and repeatability
Some systems let you adjust how output tokens are selected. Settings that favor more predictable continuations can reduce variation, while others produce more varied responses. A fixed setting or seed, when supported, may help comparison, but identical requests are not guaranteed to yield identical results across services, model versions, or configurations.
Record the model identifier, relevant settings, prompt or instruction version, input article identifier, and date for each evaluation run. Keep test examples stable when comparing changes. If a model version changes, recheck the behavior rather than assuming that a previously successful prompt still works the same way.
crumbs: 5  Language Models and Generative AI

title: Language Models and Generative AI
text:
Compare against the article-summary baseline
The baseline from Chapter 03 is a manual template, possibly aided by document search. A model-assisted draft is useful only if its benefit persists after verification and correction.







Measure
Question to answer




Field support
Does the article support every substantive claim?


Completeness
Are all four requested fields addressed, including explicit missingness?


Reference validity
Can the reviewer locate the cited passage, and does it support the field?


Reviewer effort
How long does checking and correcting the draft take?


Error severity
Which mistakes could mislead a reader or change an interpretation?


Cost and delay
What does each completed, reviewed summary require?



Use representative articles held back from prompt development. Include a straightforward paper, an unusual layout, an article with qualified findings, and a case where a requested detail is absent. Compare the completed workflow, not just the time taken to generate a first draft.

title: Language Models and Generative AI
text:
Practice: specify one generation task
Write a short specification for your prototype:

User and purpose: Who will use the output, and what work does it support?
Permitted input: Which document or information may be supplied?
Output contract: Which fields, format, and source references are required?
Missing information: What should the system say when the evidence is absent?
Checks: Which requirements can software check, and which require source review?
Comparison: Which baseline and representative cases will you use?

Then prepare four evaluation cases: an ordinary case, an unusual but valid case, a case with missing evidence, and a case with a tempting but unsupported conclusion. For each, record the expected behavior before viewing a model response. Do not place private or unapproved source material into a test service.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
text:
When the input is more than text
Chapter 05 examined language models that draft or transform text. Many real tasks also involve photographs, scans, plots, diagrams, tables, audio, or video. A multimodal system can process or produce more than one kind of information, but the ability to accept a file does not ensure that it reads every detail correctly.
Consider our article-summary prototype. The article may contain selectable text, a result shown only in a figure, or scanned pages that require text recognition. If the prototype ignores these materials, its summary may omit key evidence. If it interprets them carelessly, it may report the wrong result with misplaced confidence. The workflow must record what was actually supplied and what could be checked.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
section: Define the input and output separately
text:
Define the input and output separately
The words image AI and multimodal AI cover several different tasks:









Task
Example input
Example output
Main verification question




Image classification
Photograph
Label from a defined set
Does the label match the pictured subject and task definition?


Object detection
Photograph or frame
Locations and labels
Are the objects present and correctly located?


Optical character recognition (OCR)
Scan or photographed page
Extracted text
Were words, numbers, units, and reading order preserved?


Visual question answering
Chart or diagram plus a question
Text answer
Does the visual evidence support the answer?


Image description
Photograph or figure
Caption or alt text
Does the description distinguish visible facts from guesses?


Image generation
Text instruction or reference image
New image
Does it meet the brief without misrepresenting evidence?



A system may combine these tasks. For example, answering a question about a scanned plot requires reading axes and labels, interpreting marks, and expressing the result in text. Evaluate those stages separately when possible.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
text:
Representations and visual evidence
Image systems turn visual input into numerical representations that a model can process. Some systems work with an entire image; others use patches, crops, or selected regions. A multimodal model can relate these representations to text instructions and return an answer or description.
The model’s answer remains an interpretation of the supplied pixels. Small text, low resolution, cropped axes, color legends, overlapping points, and unfamiliar notation can all affect that interpretation. A model can also draw on learned conventions to guess what a chart usually shows, even when the specific chart shows something different.
Ask a concrete question: Which part of the source establishes this claim? If the source does not support the claim at readable quality, the appropriate output is uncertainty or a request for a better source.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
text:
Scanned documents and OCR
A PDF is a container, not a guarantee that its text can be copied. A scanned article may consist of page images. OCR can turn visible characters into text, but errors in digits, minus signs, decimal points, Greek letters, units, superscripts, and column order can change scientific meaning.
Before summarizing a scanned article:

Identify whether pages contain selectable text or only images.
Extract text or apply OCR using a permitted method.
Inspect representative pages, including tables and pages with unusual layouts.
Keep page references so a reviewer can return to the original.
Mark unreadable or ambiguous portions instead of guessing.

For the article example, “0.05” misread as “0.5” is not a small formatting issue. Any result that depends on a difficult scan should be checked directly against the page image.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
section: Figures and tables require their own checks
text:
Figures and tables require their own checks
A figure can show a trend while its caption limits the interpretation. A chart may show group means, confidence intervals, individual observations, or model estimates. Without reading the axes, legend, caption, and surrounding text, a visual summary can overstate what the figure establishes.
Use the following inspection order for a figure or table:

Identify the figure or table number and its caption.
Read axes, column names, units, group definitions, and legend.
Distinguish values shown directly from interpretations in the article text.
Look for uncertainty intervals, sample sizes, exclusions, and footnotes.
Record the specific claim being extracted and its location.

If precise numerical values are needed, prefer an accessible source table or underlying data where available. Estimating a value from the height of a bar can be appropriate for a rough visual description, but should not be presented as an exact reported number.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
text:
Continue the article-summary example
Suppose the article’s main finding appears in a results paragraph and a figure. A reviewer may reasonably want both: the authors’ stated conclusion and a check that the figure is consistent with it.








Source component
What the prototype can do
What the reviewer must inspect




Extracted article text
Draft the study aim and design
Whether extraction preserved headings and meaning


Results figure
Describe visible comparisons
Axes, scale, groups, uncertainty, and caption


Data table
Copy requested values
Exact cells, units, footnotes, and missing values


Discussion section
Identify stated limitations
Whether limitations are attributed to the authors



The draft should distinguish “the authors report” from “the figure appears to show.” It should not turn a visual association into a causal claim. If a figure cannot be read reliably, the prototype can flag it for manual review while still completing fields supported by readable text.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
section: Images used as input versus images generated as output
text:
Images used as input versus images generated as output
A generated illustration may help explain an idea or communicate a proposed design. It is not evidence that a pictured person, event, experiment, or observation exists. The same distinction matters when generating a chart: an attractive chart is only meaningful if its labels, numbers, and relationships come from verified data.
For research communication, keep the source of each visual clear. Use actual source figures and data when reporting findings, subject to permission and attribution requirements. Use generated images for clearly identified conceptual illustrations when they serve the reader. Do not rely on image generation for exact labels, data relationships, or scientific measurements.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
text:
A practical modality plan
Before adding a visual model, write down the pathway for each input:









Input
Proposed handling
Evidence retained
Failure response




Selectable article text
Extract and preserve section boundaries
Article and section reference
Flag extraction gaps


Scanned page
OCR and page-level inspection
Original page number and image
Flag unreadable content


Figure
Read caption, axes, and marked values
Figure number and location
Ask for review if ambiguous


Table
Parse or transcribe relevant cells
Table number, row, column, and units
Flag uncertain cells



Include only modalities that solve a real problem in the first prototype. If the articles selected for the initial test are text-only, a text workflow may be the sensible first version. Add figures or scans when the use case needs them and you can evaluate them properly.

title: Image and Multimodal AI
section: Build evaluation cases that expose visual errors

title: Image and Multimodal AI
section: Practice: write a modality and evidence plan
text:
Practice: write a modality and evidence plan
For your prototype, answer these questions:

Which inputs are text, images, audio, or a mixture? Are all of them necessary?
How will each input be converted into a form the system can use?
Which important details could be lost during extraction or resizing?
What source location will accompany each output claim?
Which claims can be checked mechanically, and which need a person?
When should the system say that it cannot read or interpret the input?

Write one test case in which the content is legible and one in which it is not. Describe the expected behavior in both cases. This simple exercise prevents “file accepted” from being confused with “evidence understood.”

text:

I understand that OCR, figure interpretation, and image generation require different checks.
